name: Vibravox
description: A dataset compliant with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) containing audio recordings using five different body-conduction audio sensors: two in-ear microphones, two bone conduction vibration pickups, and a laryngophone. The dataset also includes audio data from an airborne microphone used as a reference. The Vibravox corpus contains 45 hours per sensor of speech samples and physiological sounds recorded by 188 participants under different acoustic conditions imposed by a high order ambisonics 3D spatializer.

creator.name: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poirée, Véronique Zimpfer, and Éric Bavu
creator.affiliation: Laboratoire de Mécanique des Structures et des Systèmes Couplés, Conservatoire national des arts et métiers, HESAM Université, 75003 Paris, France; French-German Research Institute of Saint-Louis (ISL)

citeAs: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poirée, Véronique Zimpfer, and Éric Bavu. Vibravox: A Dataset of French Speech Captured with Body-conduction Audio Sensors. Submitted to Elsevier Speech Communication, 2024.
rai:dataCollection: A total of 200 participants contributed to the dataset, with 188 retained after post-processing to ensure high-quality data. The recording process consists of four steps performed consecutively for each participant: speech-clean (15 minutes of reading sentences), speechless-noisy (2 minutes 24 seconds of silence in noisy environment), speechless-clean (54 seconds of silence in complete silence), and speech-noisy (54 seconds of reading in noisy environment). Participants were equipped with six audio sensors simultaneously: a headset microphone, forehead accelerometer, in-ear soft foam microphone, in-ear rigid earpiece microphone, throat microphone, and temple vibration pickup. The Zoom F8n field recorder was used to record all six sensor signals simultaneously at a sampling rate of 48 kHz and a resolution of 32 bits.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The text utilized for participant readings originates from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice. This textual data was further filtered to produce a simplified dataset with a minimum number of textual and phonemic symbols and to minimize pronunciation uncertainty. Audio recordings were obtained from sensors worn by participants during the broadcast of 3D spatialized ambient noise. A significant proportion of the noise excerpts were sourced from the Audio Set, with a particular focus on noise classes relevant to BCMs applications, such as those encountered in battlefield and industrial environments. In-house recordings of concerts and street events in 3rd and 5th order ambisonics were also rendered around the participants.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Once the unwanted sentences were removed, common text normalization operations were applied, such as lowercasing text and removing punctuation except for apostrophes. From this normalized text, the corresponding phonetic transcription was generated using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA), which contains 33 phonemes in French. This operation was done with the text phonemizer of the CoML lab. For some words, the phonemizer produced some language switches that were avoided. A phase of manual phonetic transcription was then necessary for these unrecognized words.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A series of three automatic filters were applied to remove utterances with obvious deficiencies. The filtering process comprises two main stages: extracting indicators for evaluating audio capture quality, and using these indicators to derive a set of filters. The whisper-timestamped model was used for speech-to-text and voice activity detection. Three filters were employed: (1) discarding audio samples where PER > 10%, (2) verifying sensor functionality by examining the ratio between speech and silence energy levels (SNR > 1.5 dB), and (3) detecting potential sensitivity drift on the sensors. A 20 Hz high-pass filter is uniformly applied to each acquisition channel. Voice Activity Detection timestamps were extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides, and in rare cases where adjusted timestamps exceeded original audio boundaries, audio was trimmed by 15 ms on the affected side. Out of 200 participants, 188 were retained, with a total of 28,471 sentences.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Linguistic transcriptions are included in the corpus. The text utilized for participant readings originates from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice. Phonetic transcription using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) was generated, containing 33 phonemes in French. Manual phonetic transcription was necessary for words not recognized by the automatic phonemizer.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Text phonemizer of the CoML lab, whisper-timestamped model
rai:machineAnnotationTools: whisper-timestamped model for speech-to-text and voice activity detection, text phonemizer of the CoML lab for phonetic transcription
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Age and gender information were collected. The dataset includes 97 female and 91 male participants. Mean age for females is 25.9 years (median 22, range 19-59), and for males 31.4 years (median 27, range 18-82).
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset enables overcoming current limitations of body conduction sensors for speech capture in noisy environments, with potential applications in military operations, industrial settings, access control, intelligence gathering, and battlefield forensics. The technology could be made available to a wider audience for speech capture and communication in noisy environments.
rai:dataLimitations: The limited bandwidth of speech captured by body-conduction sensors has restricted their widespread use. Body-conduction sensors are unable to capture the full bandwidth of the speech signal due to the inherent low-pass filtering of tissues. In some cases, such as when a participant's ear canal was too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing, filtering was not triggered. The dataset is only available in French, restricting research primarily to this language. The assumption that airborne and body-transmitted speech share identical excitation sources and possess a simple transfer function between them is inadequate; producing realistic synthetic data is therefore still a challenging task.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset can be used for training and evaluation of deep learning models in three key tasks: bandwidth extension (speech enhancement), speech recognition (speech-to-phonemes), and speaker verification. The dataset is split by speaker, with 80% of male and female speakers in the training set, 10% in the development/validation set, and 10% in the test set. The dataset contains four subsets: speech-clean (for training), speechless-noisy (for data augmentation and testing noise resilience), speechless-clean (for analyzing noise properties and physiological signals), and speech-noisy (for testing systems in real-world noisy scenarios).
